title: Hydration Strategies
description: Master hydration techniques to coordinate server-side and client-side data in React Query.

data.text: Hydration is the process of transferring server-fetched data into the client-side React Query cache. When done correctly, hydration makes your app feel instant because the client never needs to refetch data that the server already loaded.

In React Query, hydration means calling `hydrate` with the serialized cache state from the server. This merges the server data into the client QueryClient before any components render. As a result, `useQuery` immediately returns the server data instead of showing a loading state.
Hydration is the bridge between server-fetched data and client-side interactivity. Done poorly, it causes waterfalls. Done well, it makes your app feel like it never needed to fetch at all.

A hydration mismatch happens when the server-rendered HTML does not match the client's initial render. React Query's hydration system prevents this by ensuring cached data is available synchronously. However, you must still follow strict rules to avoid subtle bugs.

data.title: Correct Hydration Pattern
data.content: Using HydrationBoundary for safe hydration with a configured QueryClient

data.title: Consistent Query Keys
data.text: Use identical query keys on the server and client. A mismatch between `['user', id]` on the server and `['user', String(id)]` on the client creates a cache miss and forces a refetch.

Server-side, you can prefetch multiple queries in parallel using `Promise.all`. This is critical for avoiding waterfalls where each query waits for the previous one to finish. Parallel fetching reduces total server response time and improves Time to First Byte (TTFB).

data.text: Server-fetched data should generally have a longer `staleTime` because it was just fetched. Setting `staleTime` to a few minutes ensures the client does not immediately refetch fresh data. However, `gcTime` controls how long inactive data stays in memory, so balance these based on your app's memory constraints.

Inactive data retained in cache before garbage collection
Avoid refetching if data was just hydrated
Refetch when user returns to tab

data.title: Memory Leaks
data.text: Setting `gcTime` to Infinity keeps data forever, which can cause memory leaks in long-running apps. Use a reasonable value like 30 minutes unless you have a specific reason to extend it.

You do not need to hydrate every query. If a query is only used client-side or depends on user interaction, skip it during SSR. Partial hydration reduces serialized payload size and keeps your initial HTML focused on above-the-fold content.

data.title: Selective Hydration
Implement Parallel Hydration for a Dashboard
data.description: Your dashboard page needs three widgets: revenue, active users, and recent orders. Currently they fetch sequentially on the server. Refactor to use parallel prefetching.
steps: Identify all three queries currently fetched sequentially
Wrap them in Promise.all inside the Server Component
Ensure all three share a single QueryClient instance
Set staleTime to 5 minutes for all three queries
Verify in DevTools that all three queries have the same fetch timestamp
data.expectedOutcome: All three queries fetch in parallel on the server. The client hydrates all three instantly.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Hydration transfers server cache to the client
Use identical query keys to prevent cache misses
Match staleTime to data freshness needs
Guard against memory leaks with reasonable gcTime
data.takeaway: Proper hydration ensures zero duplicate requests and instant client-side rendering.
